totals.ieepaCollectedNote: Estimated IEEPA tariffs paid by the importer class, Feb 1, 2025 to Feb 19, 2026, as reported from the Court of International Trade class certification in Freestyle World v. United States.
totals.mayStayNote: The court's rough estimate of refunds that would otherwise stay with the government, much of it tied to liquidated entries of importers that never sued.

milestones.label: Mid Sep 2026
milestones.measure: Certified and sent to Treasury for payment, including interest

milestones.label: Oct 2, 2026
milestones.measure: Refunds and interest sent to Treasury for payment

timeline.label: Tariff window opens
timeline.detail: Start of the period covered by the importer class.

timeline.label: Supreme Court strikes the tariffs
timeline.detail: Learning Resources v. Trump, 6 to 3, Roberts writing: the emergency powers law (IEEPA) does not let the President impose tariffs.
timeline.dateNote: Day taken from a Feb 20, 2026 law firm Supreme Court update; confirm against the slip opinion.

timeline.label: Trade court: every importer is owed
timeline.detail: Judge Richard Eaton rules all importers of record who paid IEEPA tariffs are entitled to refunds.

timeline.label: CBP opens the refund portal
timeline.detail: CAPE goes live in the ACE portal; importers file a CSV of entries and get refunds 60 to 90 days after validation.

timeline.label: Administration appeals
timeline.detail: DOJ appeals the universal refund order to the Federal Circuit, arguing only importers who sued should be repaid. Pending.

timeline.label: CAPE Phase 3
timeline.detail: More importers can file refund declarations.

timeline.label: Class certified
timeline.detail: Freestyle World v. United States covers more than 330,000 importers who did not sue.

timeline.label: Motion to repay everyone
timeline.detail: Class counsel asks the court to order refunds to all importers of record, sued or not.

timeline.label: DOJ answer due
timeline.detail: The government's response to the relief motion is due. This decides whether the remaining non-suing importers get paid.

covered: IEEPA tariffs (the emergency tariffs the Court struck down)
notCovered: Section 232 tariffs (steel, aluminum, autos and others)

consumerRoute.summary: Refunds go to the importer of record. Shoppers who paid higher prices have no legal route to a refund from the government.
examples: FedEx and UPS say they are reimbursing customers who paid itemized tariff charges.
Consumers have filed class actions against Walmart, Target and Nike seeking a share.
No pending bill in Congress would require companies to pass refunds to customers.
